lessons.title: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding; intermolecular forces
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Chemistry — chemical bonding (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe ionic, covalent (including dative) and metallic bonding and the properties that follow from them
Use electronegativity to predict bond polarity
Explain London forces, permanent dipole forces and hydrogen bonding and their effect on boiling points
reviewNotes: Pauling electronegativities and boiling points are textbook values; check the board's data sheet.
Lattice energy is only used qualitatively here; Born–Haber cycles are not included (check the syllabus).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Types of bonding
blocks.md:
**Ionic bond**: electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice (metal + non-metal). High melting point; conducts only when molten or dissolved; brittle.

**Covalent bond**: a shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms. A **dative (coordinate) covalent bond** is one where both electrons come from the same atom (NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺). **Metallic bond**: attraction between positive ions and a sea of delocalised electrons; conducts and is malleable.

blocks.title: Polarity and intermolecular forces
blocks.md:
Electronegativity differences make bonds **polar** (δ⁺ and δ⁻ charges). A molecule with polar bonds is polar only if the bond dipoles do not cancel (symmetry).

- **London (dispersion) forces**: between all molecules; increase with the number of electrons (size).
- **Permanent dipole–dipole forces**: between polar molecules.
- **Hydrogen bonds**: strong dipole interaction between H bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on N, O or F of a neighbouring molecule (H₂O, NH₃, HF).

items.text: δ⁻ on O, δ⁺ on H

blocks.title: Explaining a boiling point
blocks.md:
1. State the structure (giant, or simple molecular).
2. Name the force that must be overcome: ionic/metallic/covalent bonds in giant structures; intermolecular forces in simple molecules.
3. Compare the **strength** of these forces: more electrons mean stronger London forces; hydrogen bonds are stronger than ordinary dipole forces.

Never say covalent bonds break when a simple molecular substance boils.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying molten ionic compounds conduct because of electrons: they conduct by moving ions.
- Calling a hydrogen bond a 'bond' within the molecule: it is an intermolecular force between molecules.
- Forgetting that graphite conducts (delocalised electrons between layers) while diamond does not.
- Thinking H₂O has a high boiling point because its O–H bonds are strong: the O–H bonds do not break.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Ionic bonding
blocks.statement: Describe the bonding in magnesium chloride and deduce its formula.
steps: Magnesium (2,8,2) loses two electrons to form Mg²⁺ (2,8).
Each chlorine (2,8,7) gains one electron to form Cl⁻ (2,8,8), so two chlorine atoms are needed.
The ions attract in a giant lattice: formula MgCl₂ (charges balance: 2+ and 2 × 1−).
blocks.answer: MgCl₂: Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻ in a giant ionic lattice

blocks.title: Example 2 — Boiling points of hydrides
blocks.statement: The boiling points of H₂O, H₂S, H₂Se and H₂Te are about +100, −60, −41 and −2 °C. Explain why water breaks the trend.
steps: From H₂S to H₂Te the boiling point rises because the molecules have more electrons, so London forces strengthen.
Water has hydrogen bonds (O–H···O) as O is highly electronegative and has lone pairs: these are much stronger than the forces in H₂S.
More energy is needed to separate the molecules, so water boils at 100 °C instead of near −80 °C (extrapolated).

blocks.title: VSEPR theory
blocks.md:
In the **valence shell electron pair repulsion** theory, the pairs of electrons in the outer shell of the central atom repel each other and take positions as far apart as possible. The shape depends on the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs.

Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs: **lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair**, so they squeeze the bond angles.

blocks.title: Shapes to know
blocks.md:
- 2 pairs (0 lone): **linear**, 180° (BeCl₂, CO₂).
- 3 pairs: **trigonal planar**, 120° (BF₃, CO₃²⁻); with 1 lone pair: **bent** (SO₂, about 119°).
- 4 pairs: **tetrahedral**, 109.5° (CH₄, NH₄⁺); 1 lone pair: **trigonal pyramidal**, about 107° (NH₃); 2 lone pairs: **bent**, about 104.5° (H₂O).
- 5 pairs: **trigonal bipyramidal** (PCl₅, 90° and 120°).
- 6 pairs: **octahedral**, 90° (SF₆).

blocks.caption: Shapes of CO₂ (linear), BF₃ (trigonal planar), CH₄ (tetrahedral) and H₂O (bent).
blocks.alt: Four molecular models: a linear molecule, a planar triangle with three outer atoms, a tetrahedral molecule and a bent water molecule.

blocks.title: Method
blocks.md:
1. Count the outer electrons of the central atom and add or subtract for the charge of an ion.
2. Each bonded atom shares one electron (a double bond counts as one **region** of electron density).
3. Divide by two to find the number of electron pairs and subtract the bonding pairs to obtain the lone pairs.
4. Name the shape from the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs. A molecule is polar only if the bond dipoles do not cancel.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Giving the shape of the electron-pair arrangement instead of the molecule: NH₃ has four pairs (tetrahedral arrangement) but its shape is trigonal pyramidal.
- Forgetting that a double bond counts as one region.
- Assuming every molecule with polar bonds is polar: CO₂ and CCl₄ are non-polar.
- Quoting 109.5° for NH₃ and H₂O.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Ammonia
blocks.statement: Predict the shape and bond angle of NH₃.
steps: N has 5 outer electrons, and three are shared with H: 3 bonding pairs and (5 − 3) = 2 electrons = 1 lone pair.
Four pairs, so a tetrahedral arrangement, but only three bonded atoms: trigonal pyramidal.
The lone pair repels more strongly, so the angle is about 107°, below 109.5°.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Sulfur dioxide and carbon tetrachloride
blocks.statement: Predict the shape of SO₂ and say whether CCl₄ is polar.
steps: SO₂: S has 6 outer electrons; two double bonds use 4 and leave 1 lone pair: three regions, so bent, about 119°.
CCl₄: four bonding pairs, no lone pairs: tetrahedral. Each C–Cl bond is polar, but the dipoles cancel by symmetry.
So CCl₄ is a non-polar molecule.
blocks.answer: SO₂ is bent (about 119°); CCl₄ is non-polar

exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE Advanced Level style
exercises.prompt: Which type of bonding holds the atoms together in a solid metal?
exercises.explanation: Positive ions are attracted to delocalised electrons.

exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE Advanced Level style
exercises.prompt: Electronegativity (Pauling): H 2.1, Cl 3.0. Find the electronegativity difference in HCl.
exercises.explanation: 3.0 − 2.1 = 0.9, so the H–Cl bond is polar covalent (δ⁺ on H, δ⁻ on Cl).

exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE Advanced Level style
exercises.prompt: True or false: solid sodium chloride conducts electricity because it has delocalised electrons.
exercises.explanation: The ions are fixed in the lattice and there are no free electrons; NaCl conducts only when molten or dissolved.

exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE Advanced Level style
exercises.prompt: Which substance has hydrogen bonding between its molecules?
exercises.explanation: N is bonded to H and has a lone pair: hydrogen bonds form. HCl has only dipole forces (Cl is too large).

exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE Advanced Level style
exercises.prompt: Match each substance with the strongest force broken when it melts.
exercises.explanation: NaCl: ionic; ice: hydrogen bonds between H₂O; iodine: London forces; copper: metallic bonds.

exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE Advanced Level style
exercises.prompt: The boiling points of the Group 17 hydrides are HF +20 °C, HCl −85 °C, HBr −67 °C, HI −35 °C.

parts.prompt: Which hydride has the strongest intermolecular forces?
parts.explanation: HF has the highest boiling point.

choices: stronger H–F covalent bonds breaking on boiling
parts.explanation: H is bonded to the very electronegative F: hydrogen bonds form between molecules.

parts.prompt: Explain why the boiling point rises from HCl to HI.
parts.model: The molecules have more electrons from HCl to HI, so the London (dispersion) forces between them increase and more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
parts.rubric: 1 mark: London forces; 1 mark: more electrons / larger molecules.
parts.explanation: The molecules have more electrons from HCl to HI, so the London (dispersion) forces between them increase and more energy is needed to separate the molecules.

parts.prompt: When HF boils, the H–F covalent bonds break.
parts.explanation: Only the intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) are overcome; the molecules remain intact.

exercises.prompt: A dative covalent bond is one where
choices: both shared electrons come from the same atom
exercises.explanation: As in NH₄⁺ (N lone pair donated to H⁺).

exercises.prompt: Diamond does not conduct electricity because
choices: all its outer electrons are used in localised covalent bonds
exercises.explanation: No delocalised electrons are available.

exercises.prompt: London forces are present in
exercises.explanation: Temporary dipoles occur in every atom or molecule.

exercises.prompt: Which is most likely to dissolve in water?
exercises.explanation: Ethanol forms hydrogen bonds with water.

exercises.prompt: The ionic compound with the highest lattice energy among NaCl, MgO and KBr is likely
exercises.explanation: 2+ and 2− small ions attract much more strongly than 1+ and 1−.

exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE Advanced Level style
exercises.prompt: What is the shape of the CH₄ molecule?
exercises.explanation: Four bonding pairs and no lone pairs.

exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE Advanced Level style
exercises.prompt: What is the H–C–H bond angle in methane (degrees)?
exercises.explanation: Four equal regions of electron density: 109.5°.

exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE Advanced Level style
exercises.prompt: True or false: the water molecule is linear.
exercises.explanation: It is bent (104.5°) because the oxygen has two lone pairs.

exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE Advanced Level style
exercises.prompt: Match each species to its shape.
exercises.explanation: CO₂ has two regions, BF₃ three, NH₄⁺ four bonding pairs, H₂O two bonding and two lone pairs.

exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE Advanced Level style
exercises.prompt: Why is the H–O–H angle in water (104.5°) smaller than the tetrahedral angle?
choices: the two lone pairs repel the bonding pairs more strongly
exercises.explanation: Lone pairs occupy more space and push the bonds together.

exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE Advanced Level style
exercises.prompt: Consider the molecules BF₃, NH₃, PCl₅ and SF₆.

parts.prompt: Which has a trigonal pyramidal shape?
parts.explanation: NH₃ has three bonding pairs and one lone pair.

parts.prompt: Which has bond angles of 90° only?

parts.explanation: The three polar B–F bonds are arranged symmetrically (120°) so the dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: State and explain the shape of PCl₅.
parts.model: Trigonal bipyramidal: five bonding pairs and no lone pairs around P; the pairs are as far apart as possible with angles of 90° and 120°.
parts.rubric: 1 mark: trigonal bipyramidal; 1 mark: five bonding pairs, no lone pairs, repulsion argument.
parts.explanation: Trigonal bipyramidal: five bonding pairs and no lone pairs around P; the pairs are as far apart as possible with angles of 90° and 120°.

exercises.prompt: SF₆ has the shape
exercises.explanation: Six bonding pairs, no lone pairs.

exercises.prompt: Which molecule is polar?
exercises.explanation: The dipoles do not cancel because of the pyramidal shape and lone pair.

exercises.prompt: The bond angle in BF₃ is
exercises.explanation: Three regions: trigonal planar.

exercises.prompt: How many lone pairs are on the central atom of NH₃?
exercises.explanation: N has 5 outer electrons: 3 in bonds, 2 as one lone pair.

exercises.prompt: The order of repulsion between electron pairs is
exercises.explanation: Lone pairs are closer to the nucleus and spread more.
